name: Lymphoma (Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin)
definition: Lymphoma is a cancer of the lymphatic system, and doctors group it into Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
overview: The most common sign of lymphoma is a painless lump, usually in the neck, armpit or groin. Fever, night sweats, weight loss and tiredness can also occur. The exact cause is unknown for both Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, although a weakened immune system is a listed risk factor for both. Diagnosis relies on a biopsy, and treatment depends on the type and stage and often includes chemotherapy, radiotherapy or targeted drugs.
causes: The exact cause of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is unknown
The cause of Hodgkin lymphoma is not fully understood
riskFactors: A weakened immune system, including from immunosuppressant medicines
A previous cancer and its treatment (non-Hodgkin lymphoma)
Past exposure to the Epstein-Barr virus (Hodgkin lymphoma)
A first-degree relative who has had Hodgkin lymphoma, which carries a small increased risk
signs: Painless swelling of lymph nodes in the neck, armpit or groin
diagnosis: Diagnosis often starts with a GP visit, and a biopsy is usually carried out if the person is referred to hospital. A biopsy is the only way to confirm a diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma, and for non-Hodgkin lymphoma a sample is usually taken from a swollen lymph node. A PET scan may be used if the specialist thinks it would help plan treatment.
treatment: Treatment of non-Hodgkin lymphoma depends on the subtype, stage and grade. Common treatments include chemotherapy, targeted and immunotherapy drugs, radiotherapy and stem cell transplant. Some slow-growing types may be monitored before treatment starts. For Hodgkin lymphoma the main treatments are chemotherapy and radiotherapy.
prevention: The causes are not fully understood, and the sources reviewed do not describe a specific way to prevent lymphoma.
seekCare: The NHS advises having a painless lump in the neck, armpit or groin, or symptoms such as fever, night sweats, weight loss or tiredness, checked by a GP, as they often have other causes. NHS 111 or the GP the same day is the route if someone feels increasingly unwell, and 999 is for severe difficulty breathing.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of lymphoma?
sections.body:
Lymphoma Action describes a lump or lumps, usually in the neck, armpit or groin, as the most common sign, and says they are usually painless. The NHS gives the same painless lump as the most common sign of Hodgkin lymphoma. Other symptoms it lists include a high temperature, night sweats, shortness of breath, itchy skin and sudden weight loss.

Fever, night sweats and weight loss often occur together, and Lymphoma Action calls them B symptoms. Fatigue is also listed, by MedlinePlus for Hodgkin lymphoma and in NHS information on non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Depending on where the non-Hodgkin lymphoma is, itching, abdominal pain, a cough or shortness of breath may also occur. Many of these symptoms have other causes, and the NHS advises having them checked by a GP.

sections.heading: What types of lymphoma are there, and what causes them?
sections.body:
Lymphoma is grouped into Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma covers many subtypes, and Lymphoma Action describes follicular lymphoma and MALT lymphoma among them. Classical Hodgkin lymphoma is a Hodgkin type. Lymphoma can also affect the skin: Lymphoma Action says T-cell skin lymphomas are the most common kind, while B-cell skin lymphomas more commonly cause skin lumps in one or two areas.

The exact cause of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is unknown, but listed risk factors include certain infections, a weakened immune system, or a previous cancer and its treatment. For Hodgkin lymphoma, UCLH says the cause is not fully understood, and the risk is slightly raised by a weakened immune system, immunosuppressant medicines or past Epstein-Barr virus exposure. UCLH adds a small increased risk if a first-degree relative has had the condition.

sections.heading: How is lymphoma diagnosed?
sections.body:
For Hodgkin lymphoma, diagnosis often starts with a GP visit. If the person is referred to hospital, a biopsy is usually carried out, and this is the only way to confirm the diagnosis. A biopsy means taking a small sample of tissue to be examined. For non-Hodgkin lymphoma, doctors usually take the sample from a swollen lymph node.

Scans may be part of planning treatment. For MALT lymphoma, Lymphoma Action says a PET scan may be used if the specialist thinks it would help plan treatment, although this is less common than for other lymphomas. It also says a scan is unlikely unless there are troubling symptoms. Because treatment depends on the subtype, stage and grade, tests that establish these matter for the plan.

sections.heading: How is lymphoma treated?
sections.body:
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma treatment depends on the subtype, stage and grade. Common treatments include chemotherapy, targeted and immunotherapy drugs, radiotherapy and stem cell transplant. Some slow-growing types may be monitored before treatment starts. For follicular lymphoma without troublesome symptoms, Lymphoma Action describes a period of active monitoring, also called watch and wait, before treatment. Active monitoring is also listed as a main option for MALT lymphoma.

For Hodgkin lymphoma, the Royal Marsden says the main treatments are chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Early-stage disease may be treated with radiotherapy alone or with chemotherapy, while chemotherapy is the main treatment for more widespread disease. NHS information also covers rituximab and brentuximab vedotin for certain cases.

sections.heading: What is the outlook, and when should someone get help?
sections.body:
Outcomes for non-Hodgkin lymphoma vary by subtype. Hodgkin lymphoma is described as responding well to treatment, and the NHS information reviewed says most people with it are eventually cured. The NCI clinician summary says most newly diagnosed adults with Hodgkin lymphoma can be cured with combination chemotherapy, radiotherapy or both.

A painless lump in the neck, armpit or groin that does not go away, or symptoms such as fever, night sweats, weight loss or tiredness, are worth a GP appointment, because the NHS advises having them checked. Someone who feels increasingly unwell can use NHS 111 or the GP the same day, and 999 is for severe difficulty breathing.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma?
faqs.a: They are the two main groups of lymphoma, and each has its own information pages from the NHS and Cancer Research UK. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma includes many subtypes, with treatment depending on subtype, stage and grade. Hodgkin lymphoma is mainly treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

faqs.q: Is a lump in the neck always lymphoma?
faqs.a: No. A painless lump in the neck, armpit or groin is the most common sign of lymphoma, but these symptoms often have other causes. The NHS advises having them checked by a GP, who can decide whether further tests are needed.

Lymphoma Action says fever, night sweats and weight loss often occur together and are sometimes called B symptoms. The NHS lists a high temperature, night sweats and sudden weight loss among the symptoms of Hodgkin lymphoma. These symptoms can have other causes, so they are best checked by a GP.

faqs.q: Does everyone with lymphoma need treatment straight away?
faqs.a: Not always. For follicular lymphoma without troublesome symptoms, Lymphoma Action describes a period of active monitoring, called watch and wait, before any treatment. Active monitoring is also a main option for MALT lymphoma. Other types are treated with chemotherapy, radiotherapy or other drugs.

The NHS information reviewed says most people with Hodgkin lymphoma are eventually cured. Treatment is mainly chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Early-stage disease may be treated with radiotherapy alone or with chemotherapy. The outlook for non-Hodgkin lymphoma varies by subtype.

keyFacts.label: Also called
keyFacts.value: Hodgkin lymphoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma and NHL are the usual names.

keyFacts.label: Most common sign
keyFacts.value: A painless lump in the neck, armpit or groin.

keyFacts.label: Other symptoms
keyFacts.value: Fever, night sweats, weight loss and tiredness can occur.

keyFacts.label: Main treatments
keyFacts.value: Chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted drugs and stem cell transplant, depending on type.

keyFacts.label: Who to contact
keyFacts.value: A GP for lumps or lasting symptoms; NHS 111 or the GP the same day if increasingly unwell; 999 for severe breathing difficulty.
